GOING TO WAR - Uber drivers tempted to the Russian frontline

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate the underground recruitment drive of Zimbabwean Uber drivers to fight on the Russian frontline for pay

Unique Selling Point:
We have exclusive access to WhatsApp networks which reveal how the recruitment of Zim uber drivers works, and what impact it is having in this vulnerable community in Gauteng, when individuals are lured with the promise of money, jobs and citizenship to the frontline of the Ukraine/Russian war where there chances of survival are slim.

Summary:
Russia is losing thousands of soldiers on the frontline in the war against Ukraine, in a combat which resembles World War 1 trench warfare in the scale of death and destruction. To bolster its war effort, Russia is recruiting vulnerable communities in developing nations, luring young men under false pretences to fight with little training and no understanding of the war for financial gain against the Ukrainian army and drones. Already there is a high-profile criminal investigation underway in South Africa against the daughter of the ex-President Jacob Zuma, Duduzile Sambudla-Zuma, as well as a Safm broadcaster, Patricia Mantula, and others for attempting and succeeding to lure young South Africans into a situation which could easily cost them their lives and which is illegal. Now we have access to a Zimbabwean community which is being duped in the same way, through a closed WhatsApp group available to uber drivers in Jozi.

Press Release:


Going to War
A years-long conflict half a world away has cost hundreds of thousands of lives. And now Russia is seeking soldiers much closer to home. Underground recruiters lure mercenaries from vulnerable communities in developing nations to face the drones and gunfire. Amongst their targets: Zimbabwean Uber drivers living and working in Gauteng. They’re promised money, jobs and citizenship… but with little training and no understanding of the war, are they being sent to a certain death on the frontline? Carte Blanche explores the recruitment methods and networks, the impact on families and communities, and asks: Who are the Africans risking everything to fight a foreign war?
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Script:


(Voice of Zimbabwean Recruit) It's bad here my brother, this thing will affect us when we come back. Dead bodies are everywhere, we jump over them on the roads. Right now, we've become used to seeing dead bodies. You see a leg, a hand, a head. We're used to it now. Maybe when we come back to Africa it will really affect us.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The war between Russia and Ukraine is a hemisphere away. Its bloody frontline is on the other side of the world. Casualties of war number over a million.
Now in order to replace their fallen troops, the Russian army appears to have spread its tentacles across the globe, as far as Africa.

(Upsound Two African soldiers) Follow my Lord! Follow my Lord! Jesus! Remember me!

(Macfarlane Moleli) For the African men who have ended up in combat, social media clips are often their only footprints. And there is no way to discover under what circumstances they were posted.

(Macfarlane Moleli) But in Johannesburg, we have found a common pattern across a close-knit group of migrants - of how men say they were recruited by people in their own community to go to Russia.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The success of these faceless recruiters lies in how they profile vulnerability. They target Zimbabwe Uber drivers who are in desperate need for help.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Visa uncertainty and financial pressures in what is at times a hostile city form the backdrop to the daily lives of foreign e-hailing drivers and shape their choices.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Our story starts on a suburban pavement in Joburg with Naadira Munshi who often travels for work. Over time she’s become close friends with two Zimbabwean e-hailing drivers who drive her to the airport. For their safety we will call them M and D. D is now in Russia.

(Macfarlane Moleli) He was like your Uber Guy? You were like -

(Naadirah Munshi) He was my Uber Guy!

(Macfarlane Moleli) This is my Uber Guy. I don’t want to go with anybody else? Where’s D?

(Naadirah Munshi) Exactly.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Oh, so it was that kind of relationship?

(Naadirah Munshi)Yes

(Macfarlane Moleli) Ok

(Naadirah Munshi) Yes

(Macfarlane Moleli) And what kind of person was he though?

(Naadirah Munshi) He was fun, he was kind, he was very funny also, you always laughed with him but also caring like he'd just go out of his way to make you comfortable, take care of you.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Naadira’s friend, D, disappeared without warning in November.
Once out of the country, he told his friends he had secretly signed up to fight for the Russian army.

(Naadirah Munshi) I was worried about him. I was concerned about what influenced his decision to go, and whether he had been informed, properly informed about some of the ramifications.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Naadira has tried to keep in touch with their companion on Whatsapp. She wants to boost his morale and help him come home. Their mutual friend, M, also an e-hailing driver, has been texting too.

(M) When they arrived, they were not doing those hard military training. So it was just just they wake up in the morning, they run and do all those small training, maybe for the first two or three weeks.

(Instructor of recruits) You move, you are pushing for your life, you need to do this to survive. If not, then consider yourself dead.

(Macfarlane Moleli) But from a distance of thousands of kilometres, Naadira and M observed in real time how D was stripped of his rights and freedom, after signing a contract with the Russian military, written in Russian, a language they say he does not understand.

(Naadirah Munshi)His passport was taken once he signed the contract and that worried me, because I knew now he kind of had committed to something. He's going into a second phase and, like, he's now a soldier for Wagner, because they were under Wagner.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The Wagner group is a controversial Russian state-funded military company which has operated in multiple conflict zones.

(M) Now he said we can even go for seven days without bathing. And food, you would be looking for meat inside the water. That's when I started panicking that no, this is bad.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Defence analyst Darren Olivier explains that the Wagner group are crafty recruiters of men.

(Darren Olivier) One of the most common is what they refer to as proxy targeting, in which, you know, these groups who are doing the recruitment have established proxies in various countries, you know, in Kenya, in South Africa, and elsewhere. And, these are people who have some level of influence locally. Often it actually is social media influencers.

(Macfarlane Moleli) This is Yeoville, a vibrant suburb in Johannesburg and also home to many foreign nationals. But it’s also become the stalking ground for recruiters looking to find men to send them to the Russian war.

(M) They know the desperation within our communities, as Zimbabwean Uber drivers, because they target Uber drivers and security guards.

(Macfarlane Moleli) We meet another e- hailing driver who was contacted directly by a man who spoke his own language. We will call him John.

(John) He told me there’s a job in Russia. They are looking for soldiers.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The recruiter laid out the terms and conditions of what seemed at first to be a great deal.

(John) That’s a package of around 34 to 38-thousand US dollars for a contract that you sign per year. Then there’s a monthly salary of 2800 US dollars. Then after that, when you get to Russia, they give you citizenship.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Okay.

(John) Then your children, they will follow you to Russia.

(Macfarlane Moleli) John tells us that about 21 of his 400-strong e-hailing community have taken the offer. We’ve been given the contact details of some of the recruiters, but they don’t answer our calls, appearing to operate below the radar.

(Automated Mobile Phone Voice)You have reached the mailbox number

(Darren Olivier) They're speaking the local languages, they're providing these, you know, very enticing videos of what life would be like in Russia, and of course, misleading videos, because it's not like that once you arrive.

(Macfarlane Moleli) This is a video of Ugandan men singing in Swahili before going to the Front line, while a Russian voice refers to them as the disposables, recruited to take the heavy fire on behalf of the Russian army. There are stories of men deployed in Russia - from Botswana, Kenya, Somalia and also from South Africa, where mercenary work is illegal.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Two groups of South African were recruited. One never made it past the airport but 17 men, mostly from Kwazulu-Natal, are still stuck in Russia.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Multiple messages between the South African 17 and their alleged recruiters show their growing fear and desperation to come home. These screenshots were provided to us by a source in contact with the men’s families. Their recruitment appears to have been facilitated by highly-placed local politicians. This week through our investigation we received this SOS message from the group.

(South African recruit in Russia) South African Government, please, help us. We want to go back home alive. We're not well we've been crying for months now. Maybe six or seven members are injured. Four months ago, they took two of our group members to front line, they never came back.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Like other African recruits, their dreams of a new start appear to have become a living nightmare. We are told some are contemplating suicide.

(Darren Olivier) Once they arrive, they effectively arrive in the freezing cold. They're given, substandard gear. They're shouted at by Russian-speaking commanders who don't give them enough training, so very often they're given only, you know, a week or two of training before going to the front line.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The e-hailing driver, John, says he was sceptical of the recruiter’s offer, especially when he asked him, how would he finally come home?

(John) He said, as soon as you take off on that plane, there’s no coming back.

(Macfarlane Moleli) So he told you without a shadow of doubt that the minute you get on to that plane, there’s no coming back?

(John) Yes, because as you land in Russia, you become a Russian. So even if you pass on, you’re going to be declared as one of the heroes of the Russian liberation or whatever that they will call it.

(Macfarlane Moleli) One of the few voices to speak out, maybe unsurprisingly, is the Ukranian Ambassador to South Africa, Dr Olexander Scherba.

(Olexander Scherba) I'll put it this way: one day your taxi driver or agricultural worker, whatever. And next day you are in a foreign country, in a foreign war, where people speak, people speak foreign language, and your life expectancy in infantry is usually around 72 hours.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Dr Scherba estimates that Russian forces have deployed about 1400 Africans on the war front and that the odds are against them.

(Olexander Scherba) It is the most dangerous place in the world and unfortunately, I don't like to use this term, but it's a meat grinder. It's, it's, it's hell.

(Darren Olivier) It’s really a case where they're not only being targeted by the Ukrainian side, but by their own side as well. And if any of them are seen to stop or retreat, the operators use that to capture or punish or force forward those recruits. It’s utterly terrifying.

(Macfarlane Moleli) This appears to mirror the story told by D, in a short note after Christmas.

(D) We’re in the bush. All entrances are monitored by the soldiers and drones. No where to escape. I think I made a big mistake.

(Macfarlane Moleli) We make contact with the wife of a e-hailing driver. She says he was recruited to be a security guard in Russia but was sent to the front line instead. Traumatised and frightened, she was reluctant to appear on camera.

(Widow of Uber Driver) Getting Russian citizenship was one of the reasons that pushed him to do that, because he thought of the kids, if they got European citizenship, then they can travel. They can work anywhere in Europe. Nothing was explained to him about wearing a combat vest or carrying a gun or training as a soldier.

(Macfarlane Moleli) She last spoke to her husband a few days before Christmas. He asked her to pray for him and then nothing, until she found out through social media that he may have died.

(Widow of Uber Driver) No one has communicated. No one has called, not even to send a message. The kids are not going to school because he was the breadwinner.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The widow says she was turned away when she went to the Russian Embassy, seeking confirmation of the death of her husband, and the money he was promised.
Like other Zimbabweans we have met, she has no hope that her government will take up her case. D’s Russian bank account has also been blocked, stopping him from moving the cash back to Africa.

(Naadirah Munshi)They said they'll pay him at the end of the training. And then once he got paid and his account was opened, his account was blocked soon after. It's kind of demoralizing…
Macfarlane Moleli: It's a scam,
Naadira Munshi: It’s a scam, it’s an absolute scam.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Olivier ties this back to the fraudulent recruitment.

(Darren Olivier) They are effectively disposable infantry, there's no requirement for their deaths to be reported, for their bodies to be sent back, for their families to be kept informed. They are ghosts.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The Ukranian ambassador is asking South Africans to oppose what he sees as human trafficking.

(Olexander Scherba) We Ukrainians, we don't speak to Russia and we don't speak to Russians. You do. Your governments do, so your governments should use this, to approach Russians and to say: Stop.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Naadira is on edge, waiting for D to make contact after a long silence. She last heard from him briefly a fortnight ago.

(Naadirah Munshi) The powers that be, you know, they know what they're doing, and they're making an African man's lives disposable, and that that should be something our governments should be stopping and should be outraged and speaking about.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 01 February 2026 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: Going to War A years-long conflict half a world away has cost hundreds of thousands of lives. And now Russia is seeking soldiers much closer to home. Underground recruiters lure mercenaries from vulnerable communities in developing nations to face the drones and gunfire. Amongst their targets: Zimbabwean Uber drivers living and working in Gauteng. They’re promised money, jobs and citizenship… but with little training and no understanding of the war, are they being sent to a certain death on the frontline? Carte Blanche explores the recruitment methods and networks, the impact on families and communities, and asks: Who are the Africans risking everything to fight a foreign war? Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Script: (Voice of Zimbabwean Recruit) It's bad here my brother, this thing will affect us when we come back. Dead bodies are everywhere, we jump over them on the roads. Right now, we've become used to seeing dead bodies. You see a leg, a hand, a head. We're used to it now. Maybe when we come back to Africa it will really affect us. (Macfarlane Moleli) The war between Russia and Ukraine is a hemisphere away. Its bloody frontline is on the other side of the world. Casualties of war number over a million. Now in order to replace their fallen troops, the Russian army appears to have spread its tentacles across the globe, as far as Africa. (Upsound Two African soldiers) Follow my Lord! Follow my Lord! Jesus! Remember me! (Macfarlane Moleli) For the African men who have ended up in combat, social media clips are often their only footprints. And there is no way to discover under what circumstances they were posted. (Macfarlane Moleli) But in Johannesburg, we have found a common pattern across a close-knit group of migrants - of how men say they were recruited by people in their own community to go to Russia. (Macfarlane Moleli) The success of these faceless recruiters lies in how they profile vulnerability. They target Zimbabwe Uber drivers who are in desperate need for help. (Macfarlane Moleli) Visa uncertainty and financial pressures in what is at times a hostile city form the backdrop to the daily lives of foreign e-hailing drivers and shape their choices. (Macfarlane Moleli) Our story starts on a suburban pavement in Joburg with Naadira Munshi who often travels for work. Over time she’s become close friends with two Zimbabwean e-hailing drivers who drive her to the airport. For their safety we will call them M and D. D is now in Russia. (Macfarlane Moleli) He was like your Uber Guy? You were like - (Naadirah Munshi) He was my Uber Guy! (Macfarlane Moleli) This is my Uber Guy. I don’t want to go with anybody else? Where’s D? (Naadirah Munshi) Exactly. (Macfarlane Moleli) Oh, so it was that kind of relationship? (Naadirah Munshi)Yes (Macfarlane Moleli) Ok (Naadirah Munshi) Yes (Macfarlane Moleli) And what kind of person was he though? (Naadirah Munshi) He was fun, he was kind, he was very funny also, you always laughed with him but also caring like he'd just go out of his way to make you comfortable, take care of you. (Macfarlane Moleli) Naadira’s friend, D, disappeared without warning in November. Once out of the country, he told his friends he had secretly signed up to fight for the Russian army. (Naadirah Munshi) I was worried about him. I was concerned about what influenced his decision to go, and whether he had been informed, properly informed about some of the ramifications. (Macfarlane Moleli) Naadira has tried to keep in touch with their companion on Whatsapp. She wants to boost his morale and help him come home. Their mutual friend, M, also an e-hailing driver, has been texting too. (M) When they arrived, they were not doing those hard military training. So it was just just they wake up in the morning, they run and do all those small training, maybe for the first two or three weeks. (Instructor of recruits) You move, you are pushing for your life, you need to do this to survive. If not, then consider yourself dead. (Macfarlane Moleli) But from a distance of thousands of kilometres, Naadira and M observed in real time how D was stripped of his rights and freedom, after signing a contract with the Russian military, written in Russian, a language they say he does not understand. (Naadirah Munshi)His passport was taken once he signed the contract and that worried me, because I knew now he kind of had committed to something. He's going into a second phase and, like, he's now a soldier for Wagner, because they were under Wagner. (Macfarlane Moleli) The Wagner group is a controversial Russian state-funded military company which has operated in multiple conflict zones. (M) Now he said we can even go for seven days without bathing. And food, you would be looking for meat inside the water. That's when I started panicking that no, this is bad. (Macfarlane Moleli) Defence analyst Darren Olivier explains that the Wagner group are crafty recruiters of men. (Darren Olivier) One of the most common is what they refer to as proxy targeting, in which, you know, these groups who are doing the recruitment have established proxies in various countries, you know, in Kenya, in South Africa, and elsewhere. And, these are people who have some level of influence locally. Often it actually is social media influencers. (Macfarlane Moleli) This is Yeoville, a vibrant suburb in Johannesburg and also home to many foreign nationals. But it’s also become the stalking ground for recruiters looking to find men to send them to the Russian war. (M) They know the desperation within our communities, as Zimbabwean Uber drivers, because they target Uber drivers and security guards. (Macfarlane Moleli) We meet another e- hailing driver who was contacted directly by a man who spoke his own language. We will call him John. (John) He told me there’s a job in Russia. They are looking for soldiers. (Macfarlane Moleli) The recruiter laid out the terms and conditions of what seemed at first to be a great deal. (John) That’s a package of around 34 to 38-thousand US dollars for a contract that you sign per year. Then there’s a monthly salary of 2800 US dollars. Then after that, when you get to Russia, they give you citizenship. (Macfarlane Moleli) Okay. (John) Then your children, they will follow you to Russia. (Macfarlane Moleli) John tells us that about 21 of his 400-strong e-hailing community have taken the offer. We’ve been given the contact details of some of the recruiters, but they don’t answer our calls, appearing to operate below the radar. (Automated Mobile Phone Voice)You have reached the mailbox number (Darren Olivier) They're speaking the local languages, they're providing these, you know, very enticing videos of what life would be like in Russia, and of course, misleading videos, because it's not like that once you arrive. (Macfarlane Moleli) This is a video of Ugandan men singing in Swahili before going to the Front line, while a Russian voice refers to them as the disposables, recruited to take the heavy fire on behalf of the Russian army. There are stories of men deployed in Russia - from Botswana, Kenya, Somalia and also from South Africa, where mercenary work is illegal. (Macfarlane Moleli) Two groups of South African were recruited. One never made it past the airport but 17 men, mostly from Kwazulu-Natal, are still stuck in Russia. (Macfarlane Moleli) Multiple messages between the South African 17 and their alleged recruiters show their growing fear and desperation to come home. These screenshots were provided to us by a source in contact with the men’s families. Their recruitment appears to have been facilitated by highly-placed local politicians. This week through our investigation we received this SOS message from the group. (South African recruit in Russia) South African Government, please, help us. We want to go back home alive. We're not well we've been crying for months now. Maybe six or seven members are injured. Four months ago, they took two of our group members to front line, they never came back. (Macfarlane Moleli) Like other African recruits, their dreams of a new start appear to have become a living nightmare. We are told some are contemplating suicide. (Darren Olivier) Once they arrive, they effectively arrive in the freezing cold. They're given, substandard gear. They're shouted at by Russian-speaking commanders who don't give them enough training, so very often they're given only, you know, a week or two of training before going to the front line. (Macfarlane Moleli) The e-hailing driver, John, says he was sceptical of the recruiter’s offer, especially when he asked him, how would he finally come home? (John) He said, as soon as you take off on that plane, there’s no coming back. (Macfarlane Moleli) So he told you without a shadow of doubt that the minute you get on to that plane, there’s no coming back? (John) Yes, because as you land in Russia, you become a Russian. So even if you pass on, you’re going to be declared as one of the heroes of the Russian liberation or whatever that they will call it. (Macfarlane Moleli) One of the few voices to speak out, maybe unsurprisingly, is the Ukranian Ambassador to South Africa, Dr Olexander Scherba. (Olexander Scherba) I'll put it this way: one day your taxi driver or agricultural worker, whatever. And next day you are in a foreign country, in a foreign war, where people speak, people speak foreign language, and your life expectancy in infantry is usually around 72 hours. (Macfarlane Moleli) Dr Scherba estimates that Russian forces have deployed about 1400 Africans on the war front and that the odds are against them. (Olexander Scherba) It is the most dangerous place in the world and unfortunately, I don't like to use this term, but it's a meat grinder. It's, it's, it's hell. (Darren Olivier) It’s really a case where they're not only being targeted by the Ukrainian side, but by their own side as well. And if any of them are seen to stop or retreat, the operators use that to capture or punish or force forward those recruits. It’s utterly terrifying. (Macfarlane Moleli) This appears to mirror the story told by D, in a short note after Christmas. (D) We’re in the bush. All entrances are monitored by the soldiers and drones. No where to escape. I think I made a big mistake. (Macfarlane Moleli) We make contact with the wife of a e-hailing driver. She says he was recruited to be a security guard in Russia but was sent to the front line instead. Traumatised and frightened, she was reluctant to appear on camera. (Widow of Uber Driver) Getting Russian citizenship was one of the reasons that pushed him to do that, because he thought of the kids, if they got European citizenship, then they can travel. They can work anywhere in Europe. Nothing was explained to him about wearing a combat vest or carrying a gun or training as a soldier. (Macfarlane Moleli) She last spoke to her husband a few days before Christmas. He asked her to pray for him and then nothing, until she found out through social media that he may have died. (Widow of Uber Driver) No one has communicated. No one has called, not even to send a message. The kids are not going to school because he was the breadwinner. (Macfarlane Moleli) The widow says she was turned away when she went to the Russian Embassy, seeking confirmation of the death of her husband, and the money he was promised. Like other Zimbabweans we have met, she has no hope that her government will take up her case. D’s Russian bank account has also been blocked, stopping him from moving the cash back to Africa. (Naadirah Munshi)They said they'll pay him at the end of the training. And then once he got paid and his account was opened, his account was blocked soon after. It's kind of demoralizing… Macfarlane Moleli: It's a scam, Naadira Munshi: It’s a scam, it’s an absolute scam. (Macfarlane Moleli) Olivier ties this back to the fraudulent recruitment. (Darren Olivier) They are effectively disposable infantry, there's no requirement for their deaths to be reported, for their bodies to be sent back, for their families to be kept informed. They are ghosts. (Macfarlane Moleli) The Ukranian ambassador is asking South Africans to oppose what he sees as human trafficking. (Olexander Scherba) We Ukrainians, we don't speak to Russia and we don't speak to Russians. You do. Your governments do, so your governments should use this, to approach Russians and to say: Stop. (Macfarlane Moleli) Naadira is on edge, waiting for D to make contact after a long silence. She last heard from him briefly a fortnight ago. (Naadirah Munshi) The powers that be, you know, they know what they're doing, and they're making an African man's lives disposable, and that that should be something our governments should be stopping and should be outraged and speaking about.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate the underground recruitment drive of Zimbabwean Uber drivers to fight on the Russian frontline for pay
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have exclusive access to WhatsApp networks which reveal how the recruitment of Zim uber drivers works, and what impact it is having in this vulnerable community in Gauteng, when individuals are lured with the promise of money, jobs and citizenship to the frontline of the Ukraine/Russian war where there chances of survival are slim.
metadata.Summary: Russia is losing thousands of soldiers on the frontline in the war against Ukraine, in a combat which resembles World War 1 trench warfare in the scale of death and destruction. To bolster its war effort, Russia is recruiting vulnerable communities in developing nations, luring young men under false pretences to fight with little training and no understanding of the war for financial gain against the Ukrainian army and drones. Already there is a high-profile criminal investigation underway in South Africa against the daughter of the ex-President Jacob Zuma, Duduzile Sambudla-Zuma, as well as a Safm broadcaster, Patricia Mantula, and others for attempting and succeeding to lure young South Africans into a situation which could easily cost them their lives and which is illegal. Now we have access to a Zimbabwean community which is being duped in the same way, through a closed WhatsApp group available to uber drivers in Jozi.
